title: Resonance & formal charge
examples: How do I know when to draw resonance structures?
What is the difference between resonance and a single structure?
Can resonance affect the bond length?

explain.say: Today we look at resonance structures in molecules. Resonance means that a single structure is not enough.
Delocalisation means that electrons are spread out over more than one atom. It is not fixed to one spot.
Benzene is a classic example of resonance. Its six carbon atoms form a stable ring. The pi electrons are delocalised across the whole ring.
The carbonate ion is another key example. Its negative charge is spread over three oxygen atoms. This is shown by resonance structures.
In reality, the molecule is a hybrid. The actual structure is an average of all the drawn resonance forms. This gives it extra stability.
The most common mistake is drawing only one resonance structure. Remember to draw all valid contributing structures to show the full picture.

faq.q: What is the difference between resonance and actual structure?
faq.a: Resonance structures are just drawings that help us understand electron movement. The actual molecule is a hybrid, meaning it has properties from all the drawings.
asks: What is the true structure then?

faq.q: Do I have to calculate formal charge every time?
faq.a: Calculating formal charge helps predict where the extra stability comes from. It helps you decide which resonance structure is the most stable one.
asks: Why do we need formal charge here?

faq.q: How many resonance structures should I draw for benzene?
faq.a: For benzene, you draw one main structure, but you must understand that the pi electrons are delocalised across all six carbons. You do not draw multiple distinct structures.
asks: Can benzene have multiple resonance forms?
How do I represent benzene resonance?

faq.q: Does resonance make a bond stronger or weaker?
faq.a: Generally, delocalisation of electrons leads to a stronger overall bond system, increasing the stability of the molecule.
asks: Is the bond stronger when delocalised?

faq.q: What if I have multiple resonance forms?
faq.a: You draw them all and then draw a double-headed arrow between them. This indicates that the molecule is a blend of these forms.
asks: How do I show multiple resonance forms?

facts: Resonance structures are theoretical drawings, not the actual shape.
Delocalisation means electrons are spread over three or more atoms.
The carbonate ion ($ ext{CO}3^{2-}$) shows resonance across its three oxygen atoms.
Benzene's stability comes from the delocalisation of its six pi electrons.

quiz.why: Resonance delocalises the negative charge, making the bond lengths and charges more uniform.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the bond order is intermediate, not exactly one.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the single ion is one stable species, not three separate ones.
wrong.3: This is wrong because resonance forces the charge to spread out for stability.

quiz.why: Delocalisation spreads out electron density, which lowers the overall energy and increases stability.

wrong.0: This is wrong because while bond character changes, the geometry is dictated by orbital overlap.
wrong.1: This is wrong because resonance is an intrinsic property of the molecule's bonding.
wrong.3: This is wrong because increased delocalisation usually leads to greater stability and less reactivity.
